text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **

Cartographer ALEXANDER DALRYMPLE, who opposed the convict settlement at Botany Bay, was born in 1737. He feuded with Captain JAMES COOK and was sacked from the Admiralty because of his opposition to the "Thief Colony at Botany Bay."
EUGENE FRANCOIS VIDOCQ was born in 1775. A French detective, he set up the Brigade de Surete -- the world's first detective agency.
SIMON BOLIVAR was born in Venezuela in 1783; he freed much of South America from Spanish control and Bolivia was named after him.
French writer ALEXANDRA DUMAS, who wrote "The Three Musketeers", "The Man In the Iron Mask", and "The Count of Monte Cristo", was born in 1802.
American aviator AMELIA EARHART was born in 1898. She was the first woman to fly the Atlantic. There is still speculation about her disappearance during a flight across the Pacific.

Australian painter and sculptor ARTHUR BOYD was born in Melbourne in 1920. His first exhibition in London was in 1960, and his works hang in all the major Australian galleries, as well as those in the United States and United Kingdom.
British drummer with 'Marmalade', ALAN WHITEHEAD, was born in 1946.
Saxophonist with 'Japan', MIKE KARN, (ANTHONY MICHAELIDES) was born in 1958.
** EVENTS **
1567 : MARY Queen of Scots was forced to abdicate and
JAMES VI became King of Scotland at the age of one.
1701 : ANTOINE de la MOTHE CADILLAC founded a trading
post at Fort Pontchartrain, which later became the city of Detroit.
1704 : Gibraltar was captured from Spain by Admiral Sir
GEORGE ROOKE.
1824 : The results of the world's first public opinion
poll were published in Delaware, on voting intentions for the next U.S. presidential election.
1847 : Mormon pioneer BRIGHAM YOUNG reached the site of
the present Salt Lake City in Utah, and looking at the view over the huge valley he reportedly said - "Enough. This is the place."
1862 : MARTIN van BUREN died; he was the eighth president
of the United States and the first not to be born a British subject.
1862 : Australian explorer JOHN McDOUALL STUART reached
the Northern Territory coast after a ten-month trek from Adelaide. He arrived at a spot close to where the city of Darwin was developed.
1883 : The first man to swim the English channel (in
1875), Captain MATTHEW WEBB, drowned while trying to swim above the rapids at Niagara Falls.
1900 : The first Australian to be awarded the Victoria
Cross for Valour was NEVILLE HOWSE. The surgeon received the award for rescuing a comrade during the Boer War.
1925 : The first successful insulin treatment was
carried-out on a six-year-old girl at a London hospital.
1926 : The first greyhound racing track opened at Belle
Vue at Manchester in England.
1946 : The first subsurface atomic explosion was
detonated at Bikini Atoll in the Pacific. The blast aftermath was described as "a tremendous low-lying cloud, like a huge mountain, which obscured the entire target area from view."
1967 : The "Times" newspaper in Britain carried a
full-page advertisement calling for the legalisation of marijuana. The signatures of the four 'Beatles' were included.
1967 : President de GAULLE, visiting Montreal, made a
speech which ended "Vive le Qubec libre"; he was promptly rebuked by Canadian Prime Minister LESTER PEARSON and cut short his visit.
1974 : The United States Supreme Court forced President
RICHARD NIXON to hand over the Watergate tapes.
1979 : A gas explosion at the New South Wales Appin
colliery killed 14 miners.
1980 : British comic actor, PETER SELLERS, died after a

heart attack. He was 55. SELLERS was in London for a reunion dinner with fellow "Goons", SPIKE MILLIGAN and HARRY SECOMBE. SELLERS was also scheduled to undergo an important heart operation. He began his 30-year career on radio and made the
transition to the big screen in the late 1950s. His film successes included "The Pink Panther" series, and "A Shot in the Dark".
1987 : Multi-millionaire author, JEFFREY ARCHER, won

$920,000 in damages against the 'Star' newspaper. It was the highest amount ever awarded in a British libel action. The jury at the Royal Courts of Justice found that ARCHER had not paid a prostitute $129 for sex. ARCHER resigned from his position as deputy chairman of the Conservative Party when he admitted paying the prostitute more than $3,000 to avoid a possible
scandal. ARCHER maintained he had not paid for sex.
1987 : Queensland-based entrepreneur CHRISTOPHER SKASE
bought the Channel Seven television network. SKASE's Qintex group bought the Seven stations in Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne for $780 million.
1989 : Japan's Liberal Democratic party was defeated for
the first time in 30 years. The party had been dogged by scandal for several months, forcing the resignation of two prime ministers.
1990 : U.S. warships in the Gulf were placed on alert
after Iraq massed nearly 30,000 troops near its border with Kuwait.
1993 : Russia's central bank announced a drastic reform
of the monetary system, saying all banknotes issued up to the end of 1992 would be withdrawn from circulation.
1995 : A suicide bomber from the militant Moslem group
Hamas blew up an Israeli bus in Tel-Aviv, killing six people and wounding 32.
1996 : 57 people were killed and more than 500 were
injured when a bomb ripped through a packed commuter train in a Colombo suburb.
